stories.title: A Creator House With a Purpose: America House Wants You to Help Build a Better Country
stories.dek: Creator houses showed how much attention a group of people under one roof could capture. Dame Sydney Thackray on what America House wants to do with it, and how you can be part of it from anywhere.
stories.body:
Creator houses showed us how much attention a group of people living under one roof could capture. You followed their friendships, watched the drama, learned the dances, and came back for the next video.

But what was everyone building toward?

I’m Dame Sydney Thackray, and that question is at the heart of America House.

We saw the attention surrounding Hype House and the creator houses that followed. They brought people together around personalities and a constant stream of entertainment. The next post gave you another reason to watch. The shared destination was harder to find.

I wanted to take that ability to bring people together and give it a purpose that could last beyond the feed.

At America House, we’re asking you to watch what we’re doing, watch what we’re building, and participate yourself.

Because imagine what that attention could accomplish if even a fraction of the people watching decided to help.

A house where the next idea can become something real

America House is a creator house and a constant builder space in McLean, Virginia. We bring creators and civic technology builders together to work on making America a better place—and make the process something people want to follow.

There are personalities, friendships, disagreements, and the everyday absurdity of living and working together. You get to know the people. You also get to see what they are trying to accomplish.

A conversation about confusing legislation can lead to work on VoteImpact, which helps people understand bills, explore their consequences, and contact their representatives. Questions about where tax dollars go connect to ImpactLine, our work to make government spending easier to understand.

These are projects people can question, contribute to, and help improve.

The house gives that work a place to happen continuously. Someone brings a problem to the table. Someone else knows how to explain it. A builder starts working on a tool. A creator helps people discover it. The audience brings questions and experiences we might otherwise miss.

That is the relationship we want between making content and making progress.

You don’t have to live here to be part of it

The physical house is the starting point for a nationwide movement.

You can take a video of yourself explaining a problem in your town. Build a civic technology project. Gather your community around an issue you want to address. Bring your skills to something another person has started.

Maybe you know how to code. Maybe you know how to get twenty neighbors into a room. Maybe you’re good at asking the question everyone else has been avoiding.

There is room for all of that.

We want people across the country to see America House and recognize something they could start where they live. A gathering around a kitchen table. A local project with a clear goal. A video that helps people understand an issue well enough to get involved.

The movement grows when people take ownership of a piece of it.

A shared purpose without requiring the same opinions

America House is nonpartisan, with four shared pillars: transparency, accountability, participation, and abundance.

We want people to understand how decisions are made, see whether promises lead to results, have a meaningful way to participate, and help build a country where more people can thrive.

There will be disagreements about how to get there. Those disagreements belong in the work. We should be able to question an idea, examine its consequences, and improve it together.

Having a shared purpose gives us a reason to stay at the table.

Something worth coming back to

A video can disappear from your feed in seconds. What it inspires someone to build can last much longer.

That is what I want America House to make possible: a place people follow because they care about the people inside it, and a movement they join because they care about what we could accomplish together.

Watch us. Challenge our ideas. Bring your own.

Then pick something you want to make better, find your people, and start building. That is how America House becomes bigger than a house.

stories.title: GTA VI Is Finally Here. Look What America Did While We Waited.
stories.dek: Thirteen years after GTA V, the return to Vice City tells us how much America has changed and how good the games industry has gotten at keeping us logged in.
stories.body:
“Are we going to get GTA VI, or are we going to get World War III first?” For years, that was the kind of question people asked when the news got weird and Rockstar still hadn’t put out the game. Today, November 19, Rockstar answered the GTA part. Grand Theft Auto VI is out on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, 13 years, two months and two days after GTA V arrived. (Rockstar Games · Rockstar’s GTA V release announcement)

From a couple of pixels to a whole city

The original Grand Theft Auto came out in 1997, when only 18% of U.S. households used the internet. You looked down on tiny cars tearing through blocky versions of American cities. GTA III brought the series into 3D in 2001, and Vice City gave it a neon, 1980s take on Miami a year later. The appeal was simple. You could follow the story, or you could ignore it, steal a car and see where the road went. (The Guardian’s GTA history · U.S. Census Bureau’s historical internet data)

This time, we’re back in a present-day Vice City with Jason and Lucia, whose botched score lands them in the middle of a statewide conspiracy. In the first trailer, vertical videos show the kind of Florida chaos built for a social feed, including a guy trying to get an alligator out of a pool. That December 2023 trailer racked up 90.4 million YouTube views in 24 hours. Then a release planned for 2025 moved to May 2026 and again to November. (Rockstar Games · Ars Technica’s trailer coverage · Guinness World Records · Rockstar’s May 2026 date announcement · Rockstar’s November 2026 date announcement)

What America did before GTA VI

When GTA V came out, the iPhone 5s was still three days away. In May 2013, 56% of American adults owned a smartphone, according to Pew Research Center. In 2026, 91% did. Over roughly the same stretch, the country grew from about 316 million people in 2013 to 341.8 million in 2025. (Apple · Pew Research Center · 2013 Census estimate · 2025 Census estimate)

In those years, the Supreme Court recognized a nationwide right to same-sex marriage. NASA and SpaceX sent astronauts into orbit from American soil for the first time since the shuttle era. COVID-19 sent millions of workers home. Then ChatGPT arrived, and people started handing a chatbot their first drafts. A kid who played GTA V after middle school could be dropping their own kid off at school today. (Obergefell v. Hodges · NASA · U.S. Census Bureau on remote work · OpenAI’s 2022 announcement)

That’s why “we got ___ before GTA VI” worked. When a witness testified about UFOs in Congress in 2023, the internet’s version was, “We got aliens before GTA VI.” The World War III version gave the same joke a darker edge. The news could feel ridiculous and frightening on the same afternoon. For a second, everybody in the comments could agree on one thing. Surely the game would be out by now. (Know Your Meme)

How many copies did GTA sell?

Before GTA VI launched, Take-Two reported more than 475 million units worldwide for the franchise. Rockstar says GTA V alone accounted for nearly 235 million, including 11.21 million in its first 24 hours, according to Guinness World Records. The lifetime figures are publisher sell-in totals, which can include copies shipped to retailers. (Take-Two’s SEC filing · Take-Two’s launch announcement · Guinness World Records)

For GTA VI, analytics firm Sensor Tower estimated about 19.1 million copies sold by Thursday morning, Reuters reported. Take-Two had yet to release an official launch-day count. And in Miami on Wednesday night, the Heat played a Vice City-themed game. The real city was throwing a party for its fictional counterpart. (Reuters)

What all that time online costs

Part of the reason the wait lasted so long in public is that GTA V never really left. Rockstar brought it and GTA Online to newer consoles. Players built roleplay communities, while Rockstar kept earning money from virtual currency and in-game purchases. A game people once finished could become a place they went back to every night. (Rockstar on GTA Online’s rerelease · Rockstar’s roleplay community update · Take-Two’s SEC filing)

There’s real pleasure in that. A game can be where you catch up with a friend who moved away. It can also be where you look up at 2 a.m. and realize you have work in four hours. The World Health Organization recognizes gaming disorder when people lose control over play and keep going despite serious harm to their daily lives. It affects a small share of players. Research has also linked problematic gaming to shorter sleep and worse sleep quality. You can recognize the trade-off long before it gets that serious. What did you mean to do with that evening? (World Health Organization · Systematic review of gaming and sleep)

There’s a physical cost, too. A 2019 study estimated that the electricity used for video gaming in the U.S. was associated with 24 million metric tons of carbon dioxide a year. That was an estimate for gaming as a whole at the time. The study also found that cloud gaming can draw more energy through data centers and networks than playing locally. (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory)

So yes, enjoy Vice City. Get your friends together and see what took Rockstar thirteen years. Then give one of those evenings to the city you actually live in. Go see the friend you only talk to online, or show up for something happening down the street. The game can wait. Ask any GTA fan.

stories.title: A hacking gang says it hit Visa and Chase, and gave them 48 hours. Here’s what’s real.
stories.dek: The gang hasn’t shown any proof. Visa says a vendor was hit, not Visa. Chase says its outage was a software bug. Here’s what to do with your cards anyway.
stories.body:
The claim

A ransomware gang called n0n added Visa and JPMorgan Chase to its leak site this week, first reported by Cybernews on Nov. 17. It set a 48-hour window for negotiations before it says it will publish data it claims to have taken. It hasn’t said what kind of data or how much, and no sample has been reported.

The group was first tracked in mid-September. The week before, it claimed Expedia as a victim.

What Visa says

Visa said it is aware of the claims and that the incident started at a third-party service provider in the Asia-Pacific region. It said its own systems were not involved or affected and that there is no sign payment data, including card numbers, was compromised. Visa hasn’t named the provider.

What Chase says

JPMorgan Chase said a recent service outage was caused by a software bug and that it found no evidence of a cyberattack. It hasn’t said whether anything connects that outage to the gang’s claims. So far the only overlap reported is the timing.

What you can do today

You don’t need to cancel your cards over an unproven claim. Do check your recent transactions, turn on purchase alerts in your bank’s app, and be careful with any email or text about “the Visa breach” that asks you to log in or confirm your card. Scammers follow headlines. Go to your bank’s app or the number on the back of your card instead.

A gang’s leak-site post is not proof, and a company’s statement isn’t the last word either. The 48-hour clock runs out this week. We’ll tell you what, if anything, gets released. Do you check your bank app every day?

stories.title: First the planes. Then the banks. Now the NSA's classified network went down.
stories.dek: The spy agency's internal network failed on Tuesday, capping a week of big outages. Officials say it was maintenance, not hackers. Here's what we know and what we don't.
stories.body:
What happened

On Tuesday, Nov. 17, the National Security Agency's classified internal network stopped working, according to multiple U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News and NBC News. CNN first reported it. It's the network NSA staff use to store and share classified information inside the agency.

At the agency's headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland, non-emergency staff were told to come in at staggered times, so thousands of people wouldn't all try to log on at once while the network was struggling. Sources told CBS some work was moved to other NSA sites around the country. The gates and the rest of the campus kept running.

What the NSA says

The agency called it a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance" and said its most important missions stayed fully running. Two sources said the trouble came from routine software patching. As of the latest reports, nobody had said how long the network was down or when it would be fully back.

Was it an attack?

Officials say there is no sign of one. Two U.S. officials and a senior U.S. cybersecurity official said they saw no evidence of a cyberattack. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Tuesday that it was not an attack and not a coordinated effort by another country, and pointed to companies and agencies patching their systems.

On Wednesday in Manila, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the problems were "completely unrelated one from another" and that there is "zero evidence" hackers or other bad actors were involved.

Why people are asking

Because it's been that kind of week. Last Thursday, a worldwide Microsoft outage took down Outlook and Teams. On Friday, a nationwide ground stop held every departing flight in the country for hours. Customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and U.S. Bank hit disruptions. Apple's services went down too. Then the NSA.

Mass outages this close together are rare. But the explanations so far have a common thread, and it isn't hackers. Federal officials blamed the FAA failure on a contractor doing maintenance updates. Apple's outage was tied to an internal update. The NSA points to scheduled maintenance. Microsoft said its problem was technical, not malicious. Experts note that short outages on government networks are fairly common, often because the software is complex and not always kept up to date.

What we don't know

Why so many large systems failed in the same few days. Officials say the causes are different, and we have seen no evidence that says otherwise. We also don't yet know exactly what went wrong at the NSA, or why a routine update could take down a network that is built with backups.

The scary version is a hidden attack. The likelier version is almost as worrying: the systems we depend on can be knocked over by their own updates. What would help is slower, tested rollouts, real backups, and plain answers from the agencies when something breaks. Coincidence or a pattern? Tell us what you think.
